\chapter{Introduction and Project Vision}
\section{Project Overview}\label{ch1:sec:overview}
FlakeTrace is a self-hosted command-line tool that diagnoses \emph{order-dependent} test failures
in Java projects built with Maven and tested with JUnit~4 (including JUnit~3 test classes). An
order-dependent failure happens when a test passes on its own but fails after certain other tests
have run, because those tests left shared state behind.

The developer gives FlakeTrace the project folder and the name of the failing test. In
Iteration~1 this is one command:
\begin{center}
\texttt{py -m runner diagnose -{}-project <folder> -{}-victim <Class\#method>}
\end{center}
FlakeTrace then runs controlled test orders, each in a fresh JVM, and writes two files: an
execution record of every run, and a JSON report that follows the team's report schema
(Figure~\ref{ch5:fig:datamodel}). The report gives one of three outcomes:
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{VERIFIED}: the tests responsible (the \emph{polluters}), a reduced order that
  reproduces the failure, how often it reproduced with a 95\% Wilson interval, and the shared
  resource with the exact code locations where it is written and read;
\item \texttt{CANDIDATE}: a reproducing order with a supporting resource, but a reproduction rate
  below the confidence threshold;
\item \texttt{UNRESOLVED}: no conclusion, with a typed reason such as \texttt{VICTIM\_FAILS\_ALONE}
  or \texttt{NOT\_REPRODUCED}.
\end{itemize}
FlakeTrace never changes the project it analyses: it reads the compiled classes, runs the tests
as they are, and hashes the project's files before and after every diagnosis to show this.

Its purpose is to replace the manual search developers do today, rerunning subsets of the suite
until the culprit appears, with a bounded diagnosis whose result anyone can check. It does not
detect flaky tests in general and does not repair them. Section~\ref{ch1:sec:scope} separates
what Iteration~1 has built from what is planned for later iterations.
\section{Problem Statement}\label{ch1:sec:problem}
\begin{quote}
When a Java test passes in isolation but fails after other tests have run, developers can usually
detect that the instability exists but still have no bounded, reproducible, evidence-producing way
to identify which earlier test interaction caused it and decide what to inspect next.
\end{quote}
Stated precisely: a test suite runs in some order, and one test, the \emph{victim}, fails in that
order but passes when run alone. The problem is to find the smallest set of earlier tests, the
\emph{polluters}, whose running before the victim makes it fail; to show how reliably that reduced
order reproduces the same failure; to name the shared state that links the polluters to the
victim, at the exact places in the code where it is written and read; and, when the evidence does
not support an answer, to say so with a reason instead of guessing.

Three consequences follow from this statement and shape the whole project:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The input is a known failure.} FlakeTrace starts from a failing test the developer
  already has; finding flaky tests in the first place is not part of the problem.
\item \textbf{The output is evidence, not a fix.} The result tells the developer what to inspect;
  changing the code stays with the developer.
\item \textbf{The process is bounded.} An unbounded search is what developers already do by hand.
  Iteration~1 bounds the number of orders and repeats; an explicit execution budget is planned
  for a later iteration.
\end{itemize}
\section{Problem Context and Motivation}\label{ch1:sec:context}
\paragraph{How common the problem is.} Order dependence is a major source of flaky tests in Java:
of the 422 flaky tests iDFlakies found, 50.5\% were order-dependent \cite{lam2019idflakies}. Most
order-dependent tests are victims, the case FlakeTrace starts from: Shi et al.\ found 100 victims
against 10 brittle tests \cite{shi2019ifixflakies}, and the 155 cases in RankF's evaluation are 135
victims and 20 brittle tests \cite{rahman2025rankf}.

\paragraph{How developers handle it today.} Before the proposal, the team interviewed three
practitioners: the chief executive of Inspirovix, an engineering lead at Trillet~AI and a
full-stack engineer at Learnsignal. All three described the same procedure: notice that one test
fails after others, run it alone, then rerun it after smaller and smaller groups of earlier tests
until the culprit appears. One called it ``manual binary search'' with ``no tooling support for
it''. They reported 15~minutes to an hour per incident, and up to a full working day for the worst
cases. One team saw flaky failures a few times a week but investigated the cause only once or
twice a month, because the work competes with other priorities. Their existing tools show
\emph{what} failed, not that one test changed shared state that broke another one later.

\paragraph{Why it matters.} A failure that nobody explains is usually retried, ignored or
quarantined. That wastes time, and it also hides real regressions behind ``it's just flaky''. The
practitioners also said that a tool that guesses is worse than none: in their words, ``a clearly
stated unknown is more useful than a confident but incorrect diagnosis''. FlakeTrace is designed
around that requirement.

\paragraph{Where the project started.} FlakeTrace is a Stream~B (application-derived) project: it
began from this workflow failure, not from a paper. Research tools such as iFixFlakies and RankF
are baselines it will be compared against, not its starting point (Section~\ref{ch2:sec:comparison}).

\paragraph{A limit in the evidence.} None of the three interviewed teams uses Java, Maven or JUnit;
their stacks are Python and TypeScript, and their shared state is mostly database records. The
interviews show that the \emph{workflow problem} is real. That Java teams face it rests on the
published Java studies above. An interview with a Java developer is planned after the Mid
evaluation.
\section{Project Vision}\label{ch1:sec:vision}
FlakeTrace aims to turn ``this test is flaky'' into a result a developer can check and act on: which
earlier tests break the failing test, through which shared state, how reliably that happens, and,
when this cannot be established, an honest statement of why.

The team's contribution statement places this against existing work:
\begin{quote}
Existing products mainly detect, track or quarantine flaky tests, while research tools separately
detect and classify order dependence, minimise relevant test orders, rank order-dependent relevant
tests or compare dynamic invariants. FlakeTrace contributes a self-hosted, budget-aware
active-diagnosis pipeline that combines bounded resource-event evidence with controlled
interventions and returns a statistically verified replay certificate or an explicit abstention,
evaluated against current research baselines on a frozen, project-separated Java benchmark.
\end{quote}
The project does not claim a new algorithm, and it does not claim to fix flaky tests. It defends
three properties of the complete product:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Typed abstention:} when the evidence is insufficient, the result is a named reason,
  never a guess. Built in Iteration~1.
\item \textbf{Intervention-backed evidence:} the polluters are confirmed by controlled reruns, not
  only inferred from the code; the shared resource is supporting evidence. Built in Iteration~1.
\item \textbf{Budget as a first-class input:} the tool spends a declared number of test
  executions and then stops. Planned for a later iteration.
\end{enumerate}
The evaluation named in the statement is also later work: real benchmark projects start in
Iteration~2, and the frozen held-out evaluation is in FYP-2.

has actually built. Everything outside the three supported resource families (databases, network,
caches, services, threads, timing) is recorded as unsupported evidence, never diagnosed.

\textbf{Built in Iteration~1} &
Maven project input and test discovery; environment recorded in every execution record; JUnit~4
and JUnit~3 tests run through JUnitCore, one fresh JVM per order; reproduction in the given or
discovered order, then up to 31 valid shuffled orders; victim-alone check; one-by-one polluter
search, then delta debugging to a 1-minimal set; failure-signature normalisation; 20 repeated
runs with 95\% Wilson intervals; static bytecode extraction of static fields and system
properties, including set-up, tear-down and static initialisers, at depth 1--5 with
auto-deepening; outcome decision with typed reasons; schema-validated JSON report and execution
record; source-integrity hashing; command-line tool with CI exit codes; seeded fixture suite with
written ground truth; CI on every pull request. \\
\addlinespace
\textbf{Committed, not yet built} &
Containerised runner (rootless, network disabled, resource limits, redaction of paths and
credentials); execution budget with a reserved verification share; candidate ranking and a
cost-aware search policy; filesystem paths as the third resource family; test--resource graph;
runtime evidence as a fallback where static analysis cannot explain a case (ADR-001); fidelity
to projects whose build runs suite classes; a runnable replay command in the report; frozen
benchmark of real projects with yield and exclusions; published baselines (iFixFlakies, RankF);
ablations including the depth sweep; statistics layer; reproducibility bundle; clean Linux
install from the documentation. Iteration~2 (November--January, ending at the FYP-1 Final evaluation) is committed to ranking and the adaptive policy, runtime evidence, the graph, the ablation harness, one real benchmark project end to end and a first container deployment; the rest follows in FYP-2 (Section~\ref{ch3:sec:it2}). \\
\addlinespace
\textbf{Supporting, if time allows} &
HTML report, explanation chain with evidence labels, plain-language explanation mode,
resource-coverage reporting, caching. \\
\addlinespace
\textbf{Gated} &
Certificate-Driven Remediation: for a \texttt{VERIFIED} result only, propose a patch, check it on a
disposable copy and hand the diff to a developer, who decides. Enabled only after the core meets
its Final-1 exit criteria (the FYP-1 Final evaluation). Also gated: JUnit~5, Gradle, GitHub Checks, database and network
adapters. \\
\addlinespace
\textbf{Excluded} &
Flaky-test detection as the contribution; other languages and build systems; claims of definitive
causality; automatic repair applied by the tool; hosted dashboards, team inboxes, IDE plugins,
natural-language queries, cross-project correlation; broad database or network tracing;
safe multi-tenant execution. \\
\end{longtable}
}

\paragraph{How the scope was narrowed.} Four recorded decisions shaped the table:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Proof of concept, NARROW (28 August 2026).} At depth~1, static analysis found no
  write/read overlap for any candidate in any case, and three of five pre-registered gates failed:
  reproduction yield, ranking quality, and execution saving (0\% against a 30\% target). The team
  kept the approach but changed the resource scope. A later pre-registered run under the corrected
  scope (4~September) passed all five gates, on held-out cases from one project
  (Section~\ref{ch2:sec:method}).
\item \textbf{Configurable analysis depth.} Depth became a committed, reported parameter instead
  of a fixed value of 1. It now starts at 2 and deepens to 5 when needed (ADR-006).
\item \textbf{Three resource families.} Static fields, system properties and filesystem paths are
  diagnosed; everything else is opaque.
\item \textbf{No instrumentation in Iteration~1.} After the proposal defence (approved with minor
  modifications), ADR-001 fixed Iteration~1 to controlled reruns plus static analysis, with a
  runtime agent as the Iteration~2 fallback.
\end{itemize}
Certificate-Driven Remediation was added as a gated module, not committed scope, so that the
exclusion of automatic repair still holds.

\paragraph{If the team falls behind.} The recorded cut order is: remediation first, then filesystem
evidence (reduced to unsupported evidence), then the adaptive search policy (ranked one-by-one
remains the default). The end-to-end diagnosis path is cut last. Any cut needs the supervisor's
approval before it is made.
\section{Project Modules}\label{ch1:sec:modules}
FlakeTrace is built as three modules, one per team member, each in its own folder. The modules meet
only through written contracts in \texttt{docs/contracts/}: the report schema and the component
interfaces. Table~\ref{ch1:tab:modules} summarises them; Chapter~5 gives the architecture
(Section~\ref{ch5:sec:arch}) and Chapter~6 the implementation.

\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.17\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.43\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.34\textwidth}@{}}
\caption{FlakeTrace modules}\label{ch1:tab:modules}\\
\toprule
\textbf{Module} & \textbf{Responsibility (built in Iteration~1)} & \textbf{Gives to the other modules} \\
\midrule
\endfirsthead
\toprule
\textbf{Module} & \textbf{Responsibility (built in Iteration~1)} & \textbf{Gives to the other modules} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endfoot
\textbf{Bounded search and verification} (M2, \texttt{runner/}) &
Runs tests in a given order in a fresh JVM; reproduces the failure, including shuffled orders;
checks the victim alone; finds the polluters one by one or by delta debugging; repeats the reduced
order; hashes the project; writes the execution record; provides the \texttt{diagnose} command. &
Victim, polluters, reduced order, raw run counts, failure signature, integrity result, path of the
execution record. \\
\addlinespace
\textbf{Resource evidence} (M1, \texttt{evidence/}) &
Reads the compiled classes with \texttt{javap}; finds static-field and system-property reads and
writes reachable from each test, including set-up and tear-down; matches the polluter's writes to
the victim's reads. &
The shared resource and the code locations of the polluter's write and the victim's read, or
\texttt{null} when no edge is found, plus the evidence limitations. \\
\addlinespace
\textbf{Evaluation} (M3, \texttt{eval/}, \texttt{fixtures/}) &
Computes Wilson intervals; decides the outcome and the typed reason; assembles the report and
validates it against the schema; maintains the seeded fixture suite with written ground truth and
the team's own random-order baseline. &
The final, schema-validated report; ground truth and baseline results to check the other two
modules against. \\
\end{longtable}
}

The modules depend on each other in one direction per diagnosis: the runner's polluters decide
which test pairs the evidence module analyses, and the evaluation module needs both the run counts
and the evidence before it can decide the outcome. Later iterations add the planned components of
the proposal's architecture to these modules: a project adapter and sandboxed runner, a
test--resource graph, a planner that ranks candidates within a budget, and a certificate generator,
with Certificate-Driven Remediation as a gated extension. In that design the dependency becomes a
loop: the planner's budget decisions change what the evidence module observes, which changes the
graph and so the planner's next decision.

\paragraph{What the interviews added.} The three practitioner interviews
(Section~\ref{ch1:sec:context}) turned several design choices into stakeholder requirements:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Self-hosting.} One interviewee said sending the repository to an external service
  was ``out of the question''; another said a tool that runs inside their own infrastructure
  would be easier to approve. FlakeTrace needs no cloud service, GPU or paid API.
\item \textbf{On-demand use.} One team found 5~extra minutes on every pull request already caused
  pushback, but 30~minutes acceptable when run on request. FlakeTrace is therefore run for a known
  failing test, not on every build.
\item \textbf{Typed abstention.} Two interviewees said independently that a wrong
  answer is worse than an honest refusal.
\end{itemize}
One request was deliberately not taken up: an interviewee asked for flaky tests to be
\emph{classified} by cause (environment, order or randomness). FlakeTrace starts from a failure
already known to be order-dependent, so classification stays out of scope.

\paragraph{Other stakeholders.} The project supervisor and the evaluation panel judge the work;
one interviewee agreed to review FlakeTrace's results later and give practitioner feedback.
Because the three user classes want overlapping things, the team does not claim ``diverse
stakeholders'' as a complex-problem characteristic (Section~\ref{ch2:sec:ccp}).

\paragraph{How results will be judged.} The statistical rules are fixed before any results are
seen: comparisons are paired by project, because tests within one project are not independent;
results are reported with bootstrap confidence intervals and an effect size, not p-values alone;
and excluded or timed-out cases stay in the yield and failure analysis instead of disappearing from
the denominator. The thresholds above are frozen before the held-out evaluation, because changing
them after seeing results would invalidate it.

\paragraph{A note on the verification rule.} The rule implemented in \texttt{eval/outcome.py} is
the lower bound alone. With the team's own \texttt{eval.stats.wilson\_interval}, 18 of 20 gives a
lower bound of 0.699, 19 gives 0.764 and 20 gives 0.839, so at least 19 of 20 are needed. An earlier
statement of the rule as ``at least 18 of 20'' was corrected in the certificate contract on
12~October~2026.
\section{Constraints and Assumptions}\label{ch1:sec:constraints}
\paragraph{Constraints.}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Target projects:} Java projects built with Maven, with JUnit~4 tests or JUnit~3
  test classes. Diagnosis runs use JUnit's own \texttt{JUnitCore} in one JVM per order, not
  Maven Surefire (ADR-003).
\item \textbf{Platform:} JDK~8 or newer and Python~3.11. CI runs on Ubuntu with JDK~8; development
  is on Windows and WSL. The evidence module uses only the Python standard library and the JDK's
  \texttt{javap}.
\item \textbf{No changes to the analysed project:} FlakeTrace never writes to the project's source,
  a promise made to the defence panel, and checks it by hashing.
\item \textbf{No instrumentation in Iteration~1:} evidence is static only (ADR-001).
\item \textbf{Limits of the static evidence,} stated in every report: calls into the JDK and
  third-party libraries are not followed; reflection and virtual dispatch are not resolved; only
  static fields and constant-key system properties are modelled; the values written are not
  modelled, so a test that restores what it changed still counts as a writer; timing is not
  modelled; and missing evidence is never taken as proof of independence.
\item \textbf{Self-hosted and free to run:} no cloud service, GPU or paid API.
\item \textbf{Team and time:} three members with fixed ownership of separate folders, integrated
  only through the contracts; Iteration~1 had to be complete for the Mid evaluation on
  16~October~2026.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Assumptions.} Each assumption below is believed but not yet shown, and is stated as such.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The 31-order figure holds for Java.} It comes from a study of Python projects
  \cite{gruber2021flaky} (ADR-008). It will be checked on the real benchmark.
\item \textbf{The supported resource families cover a useful share of real failures.} FlakeTrace's
  own extractor has so far been run on one real project, fastjson, which relies heavily on global
  static configuration; this favours the assumption. The benchmark in later iterations tests it.
\item \textbf{Static analysis to depth~5 is enough for most cases.} At depths~4--5 it found the
  shared field in both fastjson cases measured (ADR-006), where the earlier test is a state-setter
  for a brittle test, but that is two cases from one project. Where it is not
  enough, runtime evidence is the planned fallback (ADR-001).
\item \textbf{Victims are the main case.} The literature supports this (Section~\ref{ch1:sec:context}).
  A brittle test fails alone, so FlakeTrace reports it as \texttt{VICTIM\_FAILS\_ALONE} instead of
  diagnosing it.
\item \textbf{Java teams face the same workflow problem as the interviewed teams.} The interviewed
  teams do not use Java (Section~\ref{ch1:sec:context}); an interview with a Java developer is
  planned after the Mid evaluation.
\end{itemize}
\section{Ethical, Legal and DEI Considerations}\label{ch1:sec:ethics}
\paragraph{Legal.} Every project FlakeTrace is evaluated on is open source, and its licence is
recorded: the proof of concept used json-iterator (MIT) and fastjson (Apache-2.0). Source code is
fetched by script at a pinned commit and never redistributed; the team's evidence contains
manifests, logs, results and its own code, not third-party source. The IDoFT catalogue
\cite{idoft} is public research data with no personal information.

\paragraph{Ethics.} Three issues apply.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Running other people's code.} Diagnosing a failure means executing the project's
  tests. Iteration~1 runs them as an ordinary local JVM process, so it should only be used on code
  the user already runs. The committed containerised runner (rootless, network disabled, resource
  limits, redaction of paths and credentials) is planned for a later iteration
  (Section~\ref{ch1:sec:scope}).
\item \textbf{Handling code and test output.} Test output can contain proprietary details or
  credentials. FlakeTrace is self-hosted, so nothing leaves the user's machine, and it never writes
  to the analysed project.
\item \textbf{Responsible claims.} A confident but wrong diagnosis can make a developer change
  working code. FlakeTrace never claims definitive causality: it reports evidence, its limits and a
  reproduction rate, and abstains with a typed reason when the evidence is insufficient.
\end{itemize}
The practitioner interviews were voluntary questionnaires about process and timing only; no
source code, credentials or customer data were requested. Two participants are identified by role
only until they confirm how they wish to be named. The team's use of generative AI is recorded in
each member's log and in \texttt{docs/08-MidEval/genai-register.md}.

\paragraph{Diversity and inclusion.} FlakeTrace is free to run and needs no cloud subscription, GPU
or paid API, so teams and institutions with few resources can use it. Diagnosing order-dependent
failures today depends on scarce senior expertise; a checkable report makes that diagnosis
available to less experienced developers. A plain-language explanation mode, aimed at junior
developers and non-native English speakers, is in the supporting scope but not yet built.
